title: The order this implementation echoes tokens in: the first submessage leads

provenance.quote: If any NLIP message containing a submessage that where the format field is 'token', the end-point must include the same submessage with the exact same format, subformat and content in its response message to the peer end-point, except when the token was initially created by the end-point.

notes: The only case in the corpus that asserts the *order* of echoed tokens, and it is a reading rather than a rule. §6.2 ¶2 says which submessages must come back and says nothing about where they go, so `expect.reply.tokens` is compared as a multiset everywhere else and an implementation that appends in another order passes. This case pins the order through `expect.reply.canonical`, which compares the whole finished message: the request's *first* submessage token leads, then the tokens of the `submessages` array in arrival order. The reason is §5.1.5, which makes the order of submessages significant — so reproducing the order the peer used is the reading most likely to mean what the peer meant. A second implementation that fails only this case and passes the rest has made a different choice and not a mistake; it should say so here rather than change its code.
